Third Normal Form101CA table in Third Normal Form (3NF) should follow these rules:The database follows every normalisation rule of 2NF; andThere must NOT be any transitive functional dependency between attributes.To learn about 3NF, we must first understand the concept of transitive functional dependency.

Third Normal Form102CWhen some non-primary key attributes are dependent on other non-primary key attributes, the table is considered to have a transitive functional dependency.SID is the primary key of STUDENT.

Third Normal Form103CIf we know the identity code of a student (SID), we will know their class (CLASS).SID  CLASSIf we know the class of a student (CLASS), we will know the name of their class teacher (CTEACH).CLASS  CTEACHTherefore, if we know the identity code of student (SID), we will also know the name of their class teacher (CTEACH).SID  CLASSCLASS  CTEACH∴ SID  CTEACH
Third Normal Form104CThis is transitive functional dependency. While CTEACH is still dependent on the primary key SID, its dependency actually comes from the dependency of CLASS on SID.

Data Privacy1185.6Data privacy concerns the collection, storage and management of personal data, such as residential addresses, personal photos and even bank account passwords.
Principle of data privacy119AWhen handling these pieces of data, we should:use the data for its original purposes only; andnot disclose the data to unauthorised people.

Access right120BAccess rights are the permissions granted to a user to perform certain operations on specific data, such as retrieve, create, update and delete.Take the following table as an example. It stores customer accounts in a streaming platform.
Access right121BDifferent roles usually have different access rights assigned.

View122CSetting views can protect the data privacy by limiting the access of certain data for specific users.If a customer service officer is responsible for matters related to film streaming only, they should have the access right to view the data of accounts with an ATYPE of 0 and 1 only.
View123CWe may restrict what data they can view by creating a view:CREATE VIEW AFILM AS	(SELECT * FROM ACCOUNT WHERE ATYPE IN (0, 1))

Participation Constraint145.2The participation constraint of a relationship specifies whether each entity of an entity type participates in a relationship or not.

Every course must be taught by one or more lecturers;Here are some real life examples of optional sides:1. An employee may or may not have any tasks at hand;2. Cardinality255.3The cardinality of a relationship specifies how many entities of an entity type can be related to entities of another entity type.They are represented by the characters besides the lines between an entity type and a relationship.

Cardinality265.3Here are some real life examples of one-to-one relationship (with any participation constraints): Each department has one department head only; and A classroom may belong to a class, while every class has a classroom.Here are some real life examples of one-to-many relationship (with any participation constraints):Each department has one or more employees; andA school has multiple classrooms.
One-to-one relationship27AIf there is a one-to-one relationship between entity type A and entity type B, it means that for each entity a, there can be at most one related entity b and vice versa.

One-to-one relationship28AA real life example is the relationship between schools and school principals:For each school, there must be exactly one school principal; andEach school principal must belong to exactly one school.

One-to-one relationship29ASince schools and school principals have a one-to-one relationship, we may store the school principal’s name as an attribute of schools, if we are NOT interested in storing any additional data about the school principals.

Data Redundancy655.4When a database stores redundant data due to being poorly designed, anomalies may occur.The following table, STUDENT is used as an example to explain data redundancy. It is used to store the data of students, elective subjects and which elective subjects each student takes.
Data Redundancy665.4The primary key of this table is SID+EID.
Data Redundancy675.4We can see multiple records for Clem in the above table, repeatedly telling us Clem is in class 3B taught by Mr Bao.

Data Redundancy685.4There are also multiple records for the elective subject ICT, repeatedly telling us ICT is taught by Mr Suen.These duplicated pieces of data are redundant and occupy precious storage space. This is called data redundancy.
Data Redundancy695.4While it is not a fatal issue when we have abundant storage space, data redundancy tends to induce the following anomalies:Update anomaly;Insertion anomaly; andDeletion anomaly.
(a) Write the table structure of the table SPORTSEVENT. This table stores the data of sports events and should include the attributes shown in the ER diagram above.(b) What is p and q?75.1
Update anomaly70AIf the student Clem is transferred from class 3B to class 3A, all three records for Clem have to be updated at the same time. Otherwise, the data will be inconsistent.
Update anomaly71ASimilarly, if Mrs Lee teaches the elective subject ICT, replacing Mr Suen, all three records for ICT have to be updated at the same time to preserve data consistency.
Update anomaly72AAn update anomaly occurs when a database with data redundancy fails to maintain data consistency after an update is made.

Insertion anomaly73BIf there is a new student Dio who has not taken any elective subject yet, his EID can only be NULL. Since the primary key of STUDENT is SID+EID and a primary key cannot be NULL, his record cannot be inserted into the table.

Insertion anomaly74BSimilarly, if there is a new elective subject Art which is not taken by any student yet, its SID can only be NULL. Thus, its record cannot be inserted into the table.An insertion anomaly refers to the inability to insert data of one entity type without having the data of another entity type.

Deletion anomaly75CIf the student Ada, who is the only student in class 3A, quits school, her record will be deleted. As a result, the data related to class 3A, such as the name of the teacher who teaches class 3A, will be lost.

Deletion anomaly76CSimilarly, if Clem and Eva, who are the only students taking History, quit studying History. Their records for History will be deleted. As a result, the data related to History, such as the name of the teacher who teaches History, will be lost.

Deletion anomaly77CMoreover, as Eva takes History only, with her record for History gone, her data, such as her name and her class, will be lost too.A deletion anomaly refers to the loss of data of one entity type when deleting the data of another entity type.

Normalisation835.5Normalisation is the process of designing database in a particular way that:Reduces data redundancy;Prevents occurrences of anomalies; andImprove flexibility.

Normalisation845.5There are different levels of normalisation which follows certain rules. Common levels of normalisation are: First Normal Form (1NF); Second Normal Form (2NF); and Third Normal Form (3NF).
First Normal Form85AA table in First Normal Form (1NF) should follow these rules:Every attribute must not contain multiple values; andThere must not be any repeating attributes.
First Normal Form86ASee the following table, STUDENT.The attribute ENAME of a single record may contain names of multiple elective subjects, i.e. multiple values. Thus, this table is NOT in 1NF.
First Normal Form87ANow ENAME is divided into three attributes: ENAME1, ENAME2 and ENAME3.

First Normal Form88AEven though each of ENAME1, ENAME2 and ENAME3 stores a single value, they are a group of attributes which store the names of the elective subjects, i.e. they are all repeating attributes. Thus, this table is NOT in 1NF.
First Normal Form89ANow ENAME1, ENAME2 and ENAME3 of each record are broken down into multiple records.This table is now in 1NF with SID+ENAME as the primary key.
(e) Modify the ER diagram accordingly.95.1

Second Normal Form90BA table in Second Normal Form (2NF) should follow these rules:The database follows every normalisation rule of 1NF; andThere must NOT be any partial functional dependency between attributes.To learn about 2NF, we must first understand the concept of functional dependency.
Second Normal Form91BA functional dependency exists between two sets of attributes when the values of one set can be uniquely determined by the values of another set.

Second Normal Form92BConsidering the above table, if we know the class of a student (CLASS), we will know the name of their class teacher (CTEACH), but not the name of the student (SNAME). The fact that CTEACH is dependent on CLASS can be denoted by: CLASS  CTEACH

Second Normal Form93BWhen all attributes that are not primary key are dependent on the primary key, the table is considered to have a full functional dependency.EID is the primary key of ELECTIVE. Since ENAME and ETEACH are dependent on EID, the table above has full functional dependency. EID  {ENAME, ETEACH}
Second Normal Form94BWhen some attributes that are not primary key are dependent on part of the primary key, the table is considered to have a partial functional dependency.

Second Normal Form95BSID+EID is the primary key of STUDENT.SNAME, CLASS and CTEACH are dependent on SID.SID {SNAME, CLASS, CTEACH}ENAME and ETEACH are dependent on EID.EID {ENAME, ETEACH}Only SCORE is dependent on SID+EID. {SID, EID}  SCORE
Second Normal Form96BIn conclusion, partial functional dependency can exist only when the primary key of a table is a composite key.
Second Normal Form97BTo remove partial functional dependency, we have to ensure that all attributes that are not primary key are dependent on the entire primary key.See the following table:
